papers.title: RAD-TFM: Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (main track)
papers.tldr: Continues training TabPFN v2 on synthetic datasets chosen adversarially by a learnable generator that is kept close to a target real-world domain. This gives up to 10.8 points higher mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline across 6 benchmarks while adding under 0.1% of the original pretraining data.
summary: Tabular foundation models are pretrained entirely on synthetic data, so the design of the data generator shapes what the model is good at. Prior work tuned the prior over generators for overall performance, but did not target the datasets a model finds hardest or a specific real-world domain.

The authors parameterize the synthetic generator and train it adversarially to produce datasets where the model's optimality gap is large, a distributional-robustness view of pretraining. A second component constrains the adversary to generate data that resembles real datasets from a chosen domain. The pipeline is model-agnostic and is applied as continued training to TabPFN v2 and TabICL v2.

On TabPFN v2, RAD-TFM improves results on 6 tabular benchmarks, with up to a 10.8 percentage-point gain in mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline, using fewer than 100k extra synthetic datasets. Applying the same procedure to TabICL v2 also helps on three major benchmarks. Takeaway: if you work with a TFM on one domain (for example clinical tables), cheap adversarial continued training on domain-aligned synthetic data is a practical alternative to fine-tuning on scarce real data. Caveat: gains are stated as "up to", and the abstract does not say how much the average improvement is or whether code is released.

papers.title: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific
papers.tldr: Fits a linear map between two models' residual streams on unlabeled prompts and uses it to carry a refusal steering direction and read-out probes from one model to another. With prompts covering the tool's region, the transferred refusal direction recovers 102% of the target's own steering effect across 110 model pairs.
summary: Steering vectors, refusal directions and probes are normally found with labeled data inside each model separately, which makes interpretability work expensive to repeat on every new model. It is unclear when such tools can be reused across models and why earlier cross-model maps sometimes failed.

The authors learn a linear map between residual streams using only unlabeled prompts, then transfer a refusal direction (tested causally by addition and ablation), a correctness direction and a sentiment probe. They test 110 model pairs from five families spanning 1B to 72B parameters, including base to instruction-tuned transfers, with specificity controls and five seeds. They also prove when a linear map should work and derive a label-free coverage score.

A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54% of the target's refusal steering and 16% to 77% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the tool's operating region raises this to 102% and 88% to 98%, while control directions recover at most 1%. The coverage score tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains past failures across domains. Takeaway: for steering-geometry work, what you fit the cross-model map on matters more than the map itself, and a coverage score can tell you in advance whether a transferred direction will work. Caveat: only linear maps and three tool types are tested.

papers.title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026, code released
papers.tldr: Trains sparse autoencoders on AlphaEarth and Tessera satellite embeddings and evaluates them with a protocol that includes a frozen random-decoder SAE baseline. It finds that monosemantic-looking features come from sparsity alone, while only a learned dictionary reconstructs well (eight times less unexplained variance on AlphaEarth).
summary: Earth observation foundation models produce dense embeddings whose dimensions mix unrelated physical concepts, which makes them hard to inspect. SAE evaluation tools built for LLMs, such as LLM judges of feature descriptions, do not work for satellite pixels.

The authors train SAEs (including BatchTopK and Matryoshka) on two Earth embedding products and score them on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concept groups, and spatial scale. Every score is compared against baselines, including an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. They also try the sparse codes for finding land-cover sub-concepts and for out-of-distribution pixel detection.

Trained SAEs beat all baselines on reconstruction; on AlphaEarth, 88% of features align with at most one of 20 concept groups, versus a median of 12 groups per raw dimension, and SAE features carry 23 to 32% of variance within a 640 m patch versus 9%. The random-decoder SAE shares the alignment and fine-scale properties, so those come from sparsity, but trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. Takeaway: any SAE paper claiming interpretable features, including on medical image embeddings, should include a frozen random-decoder control, since sparsity alone can produce clean-looking features. Caveat: the authors say neither downstream application is yet reliable enough for practical use.

papers.title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
papers.tldr: Finds directions tied to spurious reasoning from 20 original versus distractor-perturbed problem pairs, localizes the neurons and heads that write them, and edits those weights. Without training it raises accuracy on perturbed inputs by 11.8 points on average across five reasoning models.
summary: Reasoning LLMs can be thrown off by simple perturbations such as irrelevant distractors, which suggests they lean on spurious features. Finding and removing those features inside long chain-of-thought reasoning is hard.

SWEET contrasts activations on original problems and counterfactual variants to extract token-level and sequence-level behavioral directions. It then localizes the MLP neurons and attention heads that contribute along these directions and suppresses them through weight edits, using only 20 pairs. It is tested on five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks.

SWEET improves accuracy by 11.8 points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs on average, and shrinks the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracy from 17.6% to 2.5%. The analysis points to two forms of spurious reasoning, over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking. Takeaway: contrastive directions plus component localization can be turned into a permanent weight edit rather than an inference-time steering hook, which is useful when you cannot modify the inference stack. Caveat: the abstract does not name the models' sizes or report variance across runs.

papers.title: Represented but Not Used: Value-Policy Dissociation in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Shows that the values of candidate actions are linearly decodable from hidden states of LLM agents even when the policy picks a worse action. Pushing along the value read-out direction does little, but a transport learned from natural value differences shifts choices more reliably.
summary: LLM agents need to weigh the future consequences of actions, but a bad choice does not reveal whether the model failed to represent the consequences or failed to use them. Interpretability work has looked at state and plan representations, not at action value.

The authors probe for relative action values in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B on a partially observed grid task and WebShop. They compare interventions along the probe direction with Natural Value Transport, a transformation learned from hidden-state changes that arise from actual value differences, and test a closed-loop controller using the probe as a sensor and the transport as an actuator.

Action values are linearly decodable from intermediate layers, including at states where the policy prefers the worse action, which the authors call value-policy dissociation. Probe-direction interventions have limited and inconsistent effects, while the learned transport moves action preferences more consistently, mainly at later layers, and the closed-loop controller improves task outcomes. Takeaway: a decodable direction is not necessarily the direction the model uses, so steering along a probe vector can fail even when the probe is accurate; learning the intervention from natural variation is a stronger baseline. Caveat: the abstract gives no effect sizes.

papers.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026, code released
papers.tldr: Uses TabPFN and TabICL unchanged as surrogate models for Bayesian optimization on two materials benchmarks. They are highly competitive with Gaussian processes, random forests and CatBoost without kernel choice or task-specific training.
summary: Bayesian optimization loops in materials science mostly use Gaussian processes, which need task-specific kernels and can struggle with complex relationships. Tabular foundation models predict well without tuning, but it was unclear whether they work as BO surrogates.

The Prior Labs team plugs two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, into active-learning loops as out-of-the-box surrogates. They compare against a broad set of baselines (Gaussian processes, random forests, CatBoost) on two standard materials science benchmarks, and release the benchmark code.

The TFMs are highly competitive surrogates on both benchmarks without per-task training or kernel selection. Takeaway: TFMs are a reasonable default surrogate for small-data active learning or hyperparameter search loops, saving GP kernel engineering. Caveat: this is a workshop paper from the TabPFN company with only two benchmarks, and the abstract gives no numbers.

papers.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
papers.tldr: Tests TabPFN and Mitra as nuisance models inside doubly robust causal effect estimators. In complex settings they beat all conventional learners, including Super Learner ensembles, and were the only ones to approach nominal confidence-interval coverage as sample size grew.
summary: Prior-data fitted networks predict well on tables, but good prediction does not guarantee good causal estimates or valid confidence intervals. Their value as nuisance learners for causal inference had not been checked.

The authors use PFNs and conventional learners to model propensity scores and outcome regressions inside doubly robust estimators of average treatment effects, with and without cross-fitting. Synthetic and semi-synthetic settings vary confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity.

Under simple parametric setups PFNs match correctly specified regressions; in complex settings they outperform all conventional learners on accuracy and uncertainty quantification, and only TabPFN and Mitra consistently approach nominal coverage as sample size increases. At n=200 and in higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs lose coverage without cross-fitting, apparently from propensity-score overfitting by memorizing treatment labels in context. Takeaway: TFMs can be dropped into causal pipelines as nuisance learners, but keep cross-fitting on, especially with small samples. Caveat: work in progress, not peer reviewed, and no real-data evaluation.

papers.title: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
papers.tldr: Splits visual chain-of-thought into separate grounding and reasoning steering vectors taken from a source vision-language model, aligns them to a different target model, and applies each at its own stage. Training-free, it beats the strongest capability-transfer baseline by 1.86 points on average.
summary: Teaching vision-language models to reason with visual evidence (visual chain-of-thought) needs costly post-training tied to one backbone. Existing transfer methods treat the capability as one block, so their interventions also touch stages where they do not belong.

Viscot-steer extracts a grounding vector and a reasoning vector from the source-model layers linked to each capability. It aligns them to the target model's activation space and steers the grounding layers during bounding-box prediction and the reasoning layers during reasoning-trace generation. It is evaluated on high-resolution understanding, general perception and reasoning, and math visual reasoning benchmarks.

The method transfers capabilities from several visual-CoT models into architecturally different LVLMs and beats the strongest transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the main metrics. Takeaway: splitting a capability into stage-specific steering vectors and applying each only at its stage is a cleaner design than one global vector, and cross-model alignment of steering vectors is workable. Caveat: the average gain is modest and the abstract does not give per-benchmark numbers.

papers.title: Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026, code released
papers.tldr: Trains one sparse autoencoder with a shared concept dictionary plus private per-model dictionaries across ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2 and ConvNeXt, so common concepts are reusable across vision models.
summary: Vision foundation models learn overlapping concepts but in different representation spaces, so concepts found in one model cannot be reused in another. Existing cross-model methods align coordinates while keeping the concepts themselves model-specific.

GB-SAE frames cross-model interpretability as factorization: a gated bottleneck SAE learns a shared dictionary of concepts common to all models and private dictionaries for each model's residual biases. It is evaluated on ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2 and ConvNeXt.

The authors report better reconstruction, faithful shared concepts, and reuse that generalizes to unseen models and downstream tasks. Takeaway: if you compare features across several image encoders (for example multiple backbones in one medical pipeline), a shared-plus-private SAE gives one concept vocabulary instead of per-model dictionaries. Caveat: the abstract gives no numbers, so the size of the gains needs checking in the paper.

papers.title: Uncertainty, Not Concealment: A Mechanistic Reappraisal of Sycophancy in Vision-Language Models
papers.source: arXiv cs.CV, accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Med-Reasoner Workshop, code released
papers.tldr: Uses probing, activation steering and forced choice on four medical VLMs reading chest X-rays with mismatched reports. Models encode the conflict linearly but steering never makes them report it, pointing to gated uncertainty rather than hidden knowledge.
summary: In medical retrieval-augmented generation, a VLM must flag when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray. One view says these models detect conflicts internally but conceal them, which would call for different fixes than if they are simply unsure.

The authors build a three-part diagnostic: a linear probe for matched versus mismatched image-report pairs, steering along the learned conflict direction, and two-way forced choice. They apply it to four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays and also measure cross-modal attention.

The models suppress contradictions behaviorally, and a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs better than a simple CLIP model. Steering the conflict direction never produces a contradiction, forced choice does not recover one, and attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. Takeaway: a probe-decodable signal in a medical model is not proof of concealed knowledge, and steering is a useful causal check before claiming it. Caveat: workshop paper, chest X-ray only, and the abstract gives no numbers.

papers.title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.tldr: Combines activation patching, probes and steering on OpenVLA to show that negated instructions are ignored (the forbidden task ran in 79% of negated rollouts) and that goal edits only work before layer 12 or by patching every action token.
summary: Safety rules for robots are often written as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove", but it is unclear whether vision-language-action models follow them or where they represent the goal they execute.

Using the 10 LIBERO-Goal tasks, which share one scene, the authors label which goal each OpenVLA rollout executes. They combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors.

Negation had no detectable effect: OpenVLA executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A steering vector at instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts, while vectors and patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158; from layer 16, only patching every action token worked (15 of 18 at layer 24). Takeaway: where you steer matters sharply by layer and token position, and a goal probe can serve as a runtime compliance monitor. Caveat: one model, one benchmark, and small rollout counts.

papers.title: Room to Reconsider: Reply Length Decides Whether Pushback Makes Language Models Sycophantic or Self-Correcting
papers.tldr: Shows that whether pushback makes small open models cave or self-correct depends on reply length: with a 1,024-token budget Qwen3-4B fixes 43% of wrong answers, and activation steering never reduced caving without also killing self-correction.
summary: Models often drop a correct answer when a user pushes back without a reason, and this is usually treated as sycophancy to remove. But the same pushback can also make a model revisit and fix a wrong answer.

The study uses MMLU and ARC-Challenge multiple-choice questions with Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B and OLMo-2 7B, reading the final answer from option logits after a free-form reply. It varies the reply budget, probes hidden states for caving, and tries activation steering against caving.

With a 96-token budget pushback leaves Qwen3-4B accuracy flat or lower; with 1,024 tokens it corrects 43% of wrong answers and raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Hidden states predict caving only slightly beyond confidence (about 0.04 to 0.06 AUROC in three of four probing runs), and steering against caving always suppressed self-correction too. Takeaway: anti-sycophancy steering vectors can remove useful behavior, so evaluate them with full-length replies and report self-correction alongside caving. Caveat: single author, small models only.
